The ability to compare ammunition is a direct result of the invention of rifling.
Rifling was invented around the turn of the 16th century.
Rifling forces the bullet to spin as it travels down the barrel of the weapon.
Rifling greatly increases the bullet's accuracy.
At the same time, rifling leaves marks on the bullet that are indicative of that particular barrel.
Before mass production of firearms, each barrel and bullet mold was hand made by gunsmiths, making each one unique.
The first successful documented case of forensic firearm examination occurred in 1835.
In that 1835 case, a member of the Bow Street Runners in London matched a recovered bullet from a murder victim to a specific mold in a suspect's home.
In that 1835 case, the match confirmed that the suspect made the bullet.
Further evidence that the bullet maker was the perpetrator was found in his home.
The bullet maker was convicted.
As manufacturing and automation replaced hand tools, the ability to compare bullets became impossible.
The ability to compare bullets became impossible due to the standardization of molds within a specific company.
Experts in the field postulated that there were microscopic differences on each barrel left during the manufacturing process.
These differences resulted from wear on the machines.
Since each new weapon caused a tiny amount of wear, each barrel would be slightly different from every other barrel produced by that company.
Each bullet fired from a specific barrel would be printed with the same marks.
The same marks allow investigators to identify the weapon that fired a specific bullet.
